examples.problem_statement: Gutierrez, Hoffman, Imamura, Kelly, Lapas, and Moore ride a bus together. Each sits facing forward in a different one of the six seats on the left side of the bus. The seats are in consecutive rows that are numbered 1, 2, and 3 from front to back. Each row has exactly two seats: a window seat and an aisle seat. The following conditions must apply: Hoffman occupies the aisle seat immediately behind Gutierrez's aisle seat. If Moore occupies an aisle seat, Hoffman sits in the same row as Lapas. If Gutierrez sits in the same row as Kelly, Moore occupies the seat immediately and directly behind Imamura's seat. If Kelly occupies a window seat, Moore sits in row 3. If Kelly sits in row 3, Imamura sits in row 1. Question: If Kelly occupies the aisle seat in row 3, then each of the following must be true EXCEPT: (A) Gutierrez sits in the same row as Imamura. (B) Hoffman sits in the same row as Lapas. (C) Lapas occupies a window seat. (D) Moore occupies a window seat. (E) Gutierrez sits in row 1.

solution.result: the row 3 aisle seat is filled by K
solution.description: Enter the condition the question hands you: Kelly takes the aisle seat of row 3, so that cell of the grid is now occupied.

solution.operation: \text{GH chunk (H immediately behind G, both aisle)} \to \text{rows } 1,2
solution.result: G in the row 1 aisle seat and H in the row 2 aisle seat
solution.description: The G-H block must sit in consecutive aisle seats; with the row 3 aisle seat taken by Kelly, the only consecutive aisle pair left is rows 1 and 2, so the chunk lands there.

solution.result: I, L and M fill the three window seats
solution.description: All three aisle seats are now assigned to K, G and H, so the three remaining riders are forced into the window column.

solution.result: I occupies the row 1 window seat
solution.description: Fire the conditional rule triggered by Kelly's row: because Kelly sits in row 3, Imamura must sit in row 1, and the only row 1 seat left is the window.

solution.result: L and M are placed but their rows stay undetermined
solution.description: Distribute the last two riders over the two remaining window seats; nothing in the rules fixes which of L and M takes row 2, so leave that uncertainty in the diagram.

solution.operation: \text{test choices naming } L \text{ or } M: \ H(\text{row }2) \text{ same row as } L?
solution.result: L can be in row 3, so the statement need not be true
solution.description: Since this is a must-be-true EXCEPT question, hunt in the leftover uncertainty: the only slack involves L and M, and the claim that Hoffman shares a row with Lapas fails whenever L takes the row 3 window.

key_reminders: A block of two riders in consecutive aisle seats can only occupy rows 1-2 once the row 3 aisle seat is taken.
A must-be-true EXCEPT question means the credited answer merely could be false, so leftover uncertainty in the diagram is where to look.
Once one column is fully assigned, the remaining entities are forced into the other column.
common_mistakes: Pushing the inference chain past the point the rules support and wrongly pinning L and M to specific rows.
Treating the EXCEPT answer as something that must be false rather than something that need not be true.

concept.technique_name: area maximization via the square case

examples.problem_statement: The lengths of the two shorter legs of a right triangle add up to 40 units. What is the maximum possible area of the triangle?

solution.description: Recast the triangle as half of a rectangle whose sides are the two legs, which turns the leg-sum constraint into a fixed rectangle perimeter.

solution.result: the maximizing rectangle is a square
solution.description: Apply the standard optimization fact that among all rectangles of a given perimeter the square encloses the greatest area.
Turn the perimeter back into a side length by dividing by four, fixing the maximizing rectangle's dimensions.
Cut that square along its diagonal: the corresponding maximal right triangle is the isosceles 45-45-90 triangle with both legs equal to the square's side.
Halve the square's area, since the triangle is half the rectangle, to get the maximum triangular area.

key_reminders: A right triangle is half of a rectangle built on its two legs.
Of all rectangles with a given perimeter, the square has the greatest area.
Of all right triangles with a given leg sum, the isosceles (45-45-90) one has the greatest area.
common_mistakes: Reading the 40 as the rectangle's perimeter instead of half of it, giving sides of 10 and an area of 50.
Reporting the square's area of 400 rather than halving it for the triangle.

examples.problem_statement: If 2h - 4k = 0 and k = h - 3, what is the value of h + k?

solution.result: a single equation in h alone
solution.description: Because the second equation is already solved for k, substitute the expression h - 3 in place of k in the first equation.
Distribute the -4 across the parentheses so the constant term comes out of the bracket.
Combine the two h terms and move the constant to the right-hand side.
Divide both sides by the coefficient -2 to isolate h.
Put the value of h back into the second equation and solve for k.
Add the two solved values to produce the quantity the question actually asks for.

key_reminders: When one equation is already solved for a variable, substitute it directly into the other.
Distribute a negative coefficient across every term inside the parentheses.
The question asks for h + k, not for h or k alone.
common_mistakes: Dropping the sign when distributing -4 over (h - 3) and getting 2h - 4h - 12 = 0.
Stopping at h = 6 and answering 6 instead of summing h and k.

concept.technique_name: maximizing a count under a budget by trial and error
concept.sub_category: word problems / optimization under a budget

examples.problem_statement: A certain store sells two types of pens: one type for $2 per pen and the other type for $3 per pen. If a customer can spend up to $25 to buy pens at the store and there is no sales tax, what is the greatest number of pens the customer can buy? (A) 9 (B) 10 (C) 11 (D) 12 (E) 20

solution.description: Start from the case that should be best, spending the whole budget on the cheaper 2-dollar pens, and see how many fit.
Trade one cheap pen away: the freed 3 dollars buys exactly one 3-dollar pen, so the total count is unchanged.
Trade a second cheap pen away: 5 dollars buys only one 3-dollar pen, so this combination loses a pen.

solution.result: no combination with fewer cheap pens beats 12
solution.description: Recognize the trend the trials reveal: every further swap toward the pricier pen reduces the total, so there is no need to test the remaining cases.
Take the largest total produced by the surviving cases as the answer.

key_reminders: To maximize the number of items on a fixed budget, load up on the cheapest item first.
Leftover money only helps if it reaches the price of another pen.
The budget is an upper bound, so money left unspent is allowed.
common_mistakes: Assuming the leftover 1 dollar from twelve 2-dollar pens must be spent and rejecting the 12-pen case.
Picking 20 by dividing 25 by 2 and ignoring that pens come in whole units at 2 and 3 dollars.
